h: Kings, candles and a city made for wandering
p: Behind the high altar, the Trinity Chapel is where the shrine of Thomas Becket once stood, drawing pilgrims from across Europe. Henry VIII had it destroyed in 1538, and today a single candle burns on the spot. It's a simple, moving thing to stand beside after everything you've learned about the story.

Royalty rests here too. Look for the tomb of Edward, the Black Prince, with its gilded effigy, and the tomb of Henry IV and his queen, Joan of Navarre. Henry IV is the only monarch buried in the cathedral, which surprises plenty of visitors.

Allow at least a couple of hours to explore properly, more if you join a tour. If you want to experience the cathedral as a living church, Evensong is a lovely, peaceful way to hear the choir in the setting it was built for. Remember services can affect access to some areas.

The World Heritage Site doesn't stop at the cathedral. St Augustine's Abbey, founded by Augustine himself in the late 500s, is a short walk east, and St Martin's Church, one of the oldest churches in England, is just beyond it. Both are worth adding if you've caught the history bug.

Then make the most of Canterbury itself. It's a compact, walkable city with medieval lanes, independent shops and plenty of pubs and tearooms. Walk a stretch of the old city walls, relax in Dane John Gardens, admire the Westgate Towers, or hop on a punt or river tour along the Stour for a different view of the old buildings. Chaucer's pilgrims would recognise more of it than you'd think.
